questions.prompt: According to Lesson 1, what is Microsoft Purview?
options: Microsoft's unified product family for data security, data governance, and data compliance, reachable from one portal
A single screen inside the Azure portal for managing storage account permissions
A stand-alone data catalog tool, unrelated to Microsoft 365 compliance features
A free add-on exclusively for scanning Azure SQL Database
The classic Azure Purview governance service, now retired with no successor product
A reporting dashboard built on top of Power BI for tracking IT spend
questions.explain: Microsoft Purview is explicitly not one screen or one feature — it's a unified set of solutions, organized into three pillars (data security, data governance, data compliance), all reachable from one portal, that replaced what used to be several separate tools.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes exactly the misconception Lesson 1 calls out directly: 'It is not one screen or one feature.' Treating Purview as a single Azure portal screen misses that it's a whole product family spanning Microsoft 365, Azure, AWS, Snowflake, and more.

questions.prompt: An organization wants to browse and manually tag metadata for five Azure Blob Storage accounts, with no scanning needed and no budget approved yet. Based on Lesson 3's comparison table, which tier actually meets this need?
options: The free version — auto-discovery and manual tagging are both included, and scanning isn't needed for this use case
The enterprise version, because scanning is required for any metadata tagging at all
Neither tier supports Azure Blob Storage without an upgrade first
The enterprise version, because the free tier caps manual tagging at zero annotated assets
questions.explain: The free version supports auto-discovery of Azure data sources and manual classification/tagging, with a cap of 1,000 annotated assets — automated scanning is the enterprise-only capability, and this scenario doesn't need it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: if a user holds both a tenant-wide Microsoft Entra role and a Purview role group assignment scoped to one administrative unit, the Entra role ________ at runtime, making the user's effective access unscoped.
questions.explain: Lesson 4 warns this is exactly what trips people up: when a user holds both a broad Entra role and a narrower, scoped Purview role group assignment on the same overlapping access, the Entra role wins, and the administrative-unit restriction is effectively ignored.

questions.prompt: Match each Lesson 3 licensing term to its actual meaning.
right: An Azure resource tag (Production, Test, Dev) for organizational clarity, not enforced by Purview
A no-setup, automatically-available instance capped at 1,000 annotated assets, with no scanning
The enterprise tier's billing/throughput unit: 25 operations/second plus 10 GB of metadata storage by default
The fully-featured tier, including collections, automated classification, scanning, and workflows
questions.explain: The free version is the no-setup, 1,000-asset-capped instance with no scanning. The enterprise version adds collections, automated classification, scanning, and workflows. A capacity unit is the enterprise tier's billing unit — 25 ops/sec and 10 GB storage. An environment tag is purely an organizational Azure resource tag that Purview itself never enforces.

questions.prompt: A user is granted Data reader on the 'Finance' collection. No other configuration is made. Based on Lesson 6, what access does that user have on the 'Finance → Investment' subcollection?
options: Data reader as well — collections inherit role assignments from their parent by default
No access at all — role assignments never propagate down to subcollections automatically
Data reader, but only after a Collection administrator manually re-grants it on the subcollection
Collection administrator — an inherited role always upgrades one level on subcollections
questions.explain: By default, a collection inherits every role assignment from its parent. Granting Data reader on Finance automatically grants Data reader on Finance → Investment too, without re-granting it at every level — unless Restrict inherited permissions is deliberately turned on for that subcollection.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about registering and scanning data sources, per Lessons 8 through 11.
options: Registering a source gives Purview the source's address and maps it to a collection or domain, before any scan can run
A scan rule set determines which file types and classifications a scan compares the data against
An L1 scan performs full schema extraction, data sampling, and classification
Already-scanned assets stay in their original collection until the next scan runs, when a source is moved to a different collection
Multi-source connections like Azure (Multiple) can be moved between collections just like any single source
questions.explain: Registration maps a source's address to a collection before any scan is possible, and a scan rule set defines file types plus classification rules. L1 is basic metadata only — full schema, sampling, and classification is L3, not L1. Moved sources keep already-scanned assets in their original collection until the next scan. Multi-source connections (Azure Multiple, AWS account Multiple, Azure Synapse Analytics Multiple) specifically cannot be moved between collections at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a single capacity unit (CU) buys ________ operations per second, bundled with 10 GB of metadata storage.
questions.explain: A capacity unit bundles two resources into one billable number: 25 operations per second of throughput and 10 GB of metadata storage — and the two scale together.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of creating a new scan, per Lesson 9, in the correct order.
items: Open Data Map → Data sources, find the registered source, and select New Scan
Enter a name and choose a credential, such as Managed Identity
Choose the collection to store metadata in, then select Test connection
Scope the scan to specific folders, subfolders, or tables if needed
Select a scan rule set and choose the scan trigger
Review and select Save and run
questions.explain: Scan creation always follows this order: open the source and start a new scan, name it and pick a credential, choose the target collection and test the connection, scope the scan if needed, pick a scan rule set and trigger, then save and run.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 9, what's the actual difference between an L2 and an L3 scan?
options: L2 adds schema extraction with no sampling or classification; L3 adds data sampling and classification on top of that
L2 and L3 are functionally identical except L3 runs on a faster schedule
L2 only works on Azure SQL Database, while L3 works on every source type
L2 scans structured sources, while L3 only scans unstructured file types
questions.explain: L1 is basic metadata only. L2 adds schema extraction for structured file types and database tables, but still no sampling or classification. L3 goes further, adding full data sampling and classification on top of L2's schema extraction.

questions.prompt: Match each scan troubleshooting symptom, per Lesson 12, to its most likely cause.
left: Test connection passes, but the scan itself fails
The scan can't authenticate through a stored secret
A previously working scan suddenly fails after a credential change
Azure Policy blocks storage account updates
right: An exception tag for Microsoft Purview needs to be added to the policy
Update the scan configuration with the source's new credentials
Usually a network setting — private endpoints, virtual networks, or an NSG rule blocking the data path
The Purview managed identity is missing Get and List permissions on Secrets in the Key Vault access policy
questions.explain: A passing test connection but a failing scan usually points at a network setting, not credentials. A Key Vault authentication failure usually means the managed identity is missing Get and List on Secrets. A previously working scan that now fails after a credential change needs the scan updated with the new credentials. An Azure Policy blocking storage updates needs a Purview exception tag.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 13, why doesn't a table asset show any classifications right after a scan, even though its individual columns do?
options: Classifications live on a table's columns, not the table row itself — scanning automatically classifies file and column assets, but not table assets
Table assets are never classified under any circumstances, even manually
Classifications only apply to file assets, never to database objects at all
The scan rule set used for tables deliberately excludes all classification rules by default
questions.explain: Scanning automatically classifies file and column assets, but not table assets, because classifications live on a table's columns rather than the table row itself. To see a classification on the table asset's own Overview page, you have to add it manually.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about system and custom classifications, per Lesson 14.
options: Purview ships with 200+ built-in system classifications under the reserved MICROSOFT. namespace
Creating a custom classification requires Data Curator or Data Source Administrator permission on a collection
A classification rule can be built as either a regular expression or a dictionary match
Custom classification rules can run against unstructured file types like DOC, PDF, and XLSX
Simply creating a custom classification automatically makes it get applied during the next scan
questions.explain: System classifications number 200+ under the MICROSOFT. namespace, and creating a custom one requires Data Curator or Data Source Administrator permission. A classification rule matches via regex or a dictionary file. Custom classification rules only run against structured sources and file types — never unstructured types like DOC, PDF, or XLSX. And a classification by itself isn't applied automatically — it needs a classification rule, and that rule needs to be included in the scan rule set attached to the scan.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a sensitivity label can only reach an asset in the Microsoft Purview Data Map if its scope includes ________.
questions.explain: Of the four label scope options (Files & other data assets, Emails, Meetings, Groups & sites), only Files & other data assets makes a label available to Microsoft Purview Data Map, Fabric, Azure, AWS, and more — not just Office documents.

questions.prompt: Put these five steps of the sensitivity-label-to-Data-Map flow, per Lesson 16, in the correct order.
items: Create labels scoped to Files & other data assets
Register the asset's source in the Data Map
Scan the source, which applies classifications automatically
Classifications found become the trigger condition for labeling
An auto-labeling policy applies the matching label
questions.explain: The chain runs: create a properly scoped label, register the source, scan it so classifications get applied, let those classifications become a trigger condition, and only then does a built auto-labeling policy actually attach the label. The scan itself never applies a label directly — only the auto-labeling policy does.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 17, which statement correctly distinguishes Data Map, Data Catalog, and Unified Catalog?
options: Data Map builds the technical inventory by scanning sources; Data Catalog is where people consume that inventory; Unified Catalog is the modern, business-concept-driven experience inside Data Catalog
Data Map and Data Catalog are the same feature under two different names, while Unified Catalog is a completely separate product
Unified Catalog replaces the need to ever scan a source, since it generates metadata entirely on its own
Data Catalog is a subset of Data Map used only for Power BI assets
questions.explain: Data Map is the plumbing: connecting, scanning, and keeping technical metadata current. Data Catalog is the room people actually walk into to search and govern it. Unified Catalog is the modern experience inside Data Catalog that organizes everything around business concepts like domains, data products, and glossary terms.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the glossary term lifecycle, per Lesson 19.
options: A new glossary term starts in Draft status
A term becomes visible in the Enterprise Glossary as soon as it's approved, even if its governance domain is still in Draft
A policy attached to a term can apply automatically to any data product that term gets attached to
Terms move through Draft, Submitted for approval, and Published, in that order
Acronyms can't be attached to a glossary term — only the full term name is ever searchable
questions.explain: Terms start as Draft, move to Submitted for approval, then Published, in that order. A term only shows up in the Enterprise Glossary once both the term and its governance domain are published — if the domain is still in draft, the term stays hidden regardless of its own approval. Policies attached to a term do trickle down to any data product the term is attached to. Comma-separated acronyms are a supported field, resolving to the same term.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: editing an asset's description, classifications, or glossary terms requires the ________ role on the collection that asset belongs to.
questions.explain: Lesson 21 is explicit that curation (editing description, classifications, or terms) requires the Data Curator role, by design — bad curation is considered worse than no curation at all. Rating, by contrast, needs no special role.

questions.prompt: Match each curation concept, per Lesson 21, to what it actually is.
right: Applying terms, classifications, or contacts to many search results at once
Plain-language context that makes an asset understandable and more findable in search
Social proof that other people trust the asset, plus a permanent audit trail of every change
What's actually inside the asset and what it means in business language
questions.explain: Description and tags provide plain-language context. Classifications and glossary terms describe what's inside and what it means in business terms. Rating and history provide social proof and a permanent audit trail. Bulk edit applies any of these across many assets at once.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 22, how deep can business (governance) domains nest, and how many total domains can one tenant hold?
options: Up to five levels deep, with as many as 200 domains total per tenant
Unlimited nesting depth, capped at 10 domains total per tenant
Exactly three levels deep, with no cap on total domain count
Domains cannot nest at all — every domain is top-level
questions.explain: Domains can nest inside a parent domain up to five levels deep, and a tenant can hold as many as 200 domains total — a deliberate boundary that keeps the hierarchy a readable org chart instead of an unbounded tree.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 23, what are the two shapes every Purview lineage canvas is built from?
options: A rectangular dataset (node) and a round-edged process (edge)
A circle for a source and a triangle for a target
A single universal shape representing both data and the transformations applied to it
A dashed line for lineage and a solid line for ownership
questions.explain: Every lineage diagram reduces to exactly two shapes: a rectangular dataset (node) — a table, blob, or file — and a round-edged process (edge), the activity that moves or transforms data between datasets.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ADF and Synapse lineage, per Lesson 24.
options: Only Copy Data, Data Flow, and Execute SSIS Package activities report lineage from Azure Data Factory
Synapse pipelines report lineage the same way as ADF, including Execute SSIS Package
If a Copy or Data Flow activity's source or sink uses an unsupported connector, Purview drops the lineage silently with no error
Data Flow lineage shows the step-by-step transformation logic — joins, merges, and derived columns — inside the lineage canvas
For most Azure SQL, Synapse, Oracle, and Teradata sources, lineage only covers table and view-level objects, not queries or stored procedures
questions.explain: Exactly three ADF activity types report lineage: Copy Data, Data Flow, and Execute SSIS Package. Synapse reports the same way minus Execute SSIS Package, since Synapse doesn't run SSIS packages. An unsupported source or sink causes lineage to drop silently, with no error anywhere. Data Flow lineage shows which sources and sinks were involved, but not the transformation logic itself — joins and derived columns stay invisible to the graph. And for most of those database sources, lineage is table/view-level only, not query or stored-procedure level.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: by default, a Purview lineage canvas only renders ________ levels of lineage around the asset in focus before collapsing the rest into an expandable bubble.
questions.explain: The canvas only renders five levels of lineage around the asset in focus by default — any more collapses into a numbered bubble you expand on demand, so a popular table's lineage doesn't render as an unreadable wall of boxes.

questions.prompt: Put Power BI's lineage artifact chain, per Lesson 25, in the correct order.
questions.explain: Purview captures Power BI lineage in a predictable chain: Dataflow feeds a Dataset, which feeds a Report, which feeds a Dashboard — letting a consumer walk backward from a wrong dashboard number to find the responsible dataset.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 27, why can the 'Search and browse' activity count in the Catalog Adoption report be higher than the overall Monthly active users count?
options: Because a single user can be counted in both the Search and browse category and the Asset curation category in the same window, and the categories deliberately overlap
Because the report counts every page refresh as a separate unique user
Because Monthly active users only counts users who hold the Data Curator role
Because this is a known reporting bug Microsoft has acknowledged but not yet fixed
questions.explain: The Active users by feature category chart deliberately overlaps its three counts — Search and browse, Asset curation, and All (both). A user doing both actions gets counted in multiple categories, which is why Search and browse alone can exceed the overall Monthly active users figure. That's expected behavior, not a bug.

questions.prompt: What are the four parts every Microsoft Purview governance policy statement is built from?
options: Effect, Action, Data Resource, and Subject
Role, Role group, Member, and Scope
Trigger, Condition, Approval, and Branch
Domain, Collection, Source, and Asset
Allow, Deny, Audit, and Escalate
Classification, Label, Term, and Domain
questions.explain: A policy statement reads like a sentence built from exactly four parts: Effect (today, only Allow), Action (Read or Modify), Data Resource (the fully qualified path the statement applies to), and Subject (the user, group, or identity it applies to) — for example, 'Allow Read on Data Asset FinData to group Finance-analyst.'
questions.distractorExplain: Option B — Role, Role group, Member, Scope — is a genuinely real Purview concept, but it's the RBAC permissions model from Lessons 4 and 6 describing who can manage what access, not the four parts a policy statement itself is built from. It's easy to confuse because a policy's 'Subject' and RBAC's 'Member' both describe a person or group, but they belong to two different systems.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about access policy prerequisites, per Lesson 28.
options: Data use management must be switched to Enabled on the source before any policy on it is enforced
Writing and editing a policy requires the Policy author role
Publishing a policy requires the Data source admin role, assigned at the root collection
A policy statement's Effect can be set to either Allow or Deny
The same person can both author and publish a policy using a single role
questions.explain: Data use management has to be Enabled per source before any policy reaches it. Policy author can write and edit policies; Data source admin, assigned at the root collection, is the separate role required to publish one. Today only Allow is a supported Effect — there's no explicit Deny statement. And the author/publisher split is deliberate, specifically so one person can't both write and activate a policy unilaterally.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: once an access request is Approved but the underlying data access hasn't been provisioned yet, its status becomes ________ once that provisioning actually finishes.
questions.explain: The four statuses move in order: Pending, then either Declined or Approved, and an Approved request only becomes Completed once the asset is actually provisioned and the consumer can use the data.

questions.prompt: Match each built-in data quality rule type, per Lesson 30, to what it actually checks.
right: Confirms every value in a chosen column is distinct
A binary pass/fail check on whether an asset was updated within an expected window
Flags null — and for strings, also empty or whitespace-only — values in a column that should always have a value
Confirms a column's actual values match the data type Purview expects, translated through its own internal type system
questions.explain: Freshness is a binary pass/fail on update timing. Unique values confirms distinctness. Data type match confirms values match the expected internal type. Empty/blank fields flags nulls and blank strings — and changes how the other rules on that same column treat a null if it isn't defined.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 35, which chapters make up the 'trust it' step of this course's three-step shape?
options: Chapter 3 (Classification and Labels) and Chapter 4 (Catalog and Glossary)
Chapter 1 (Purview Foundations) and Chapter 2 (The Data Map)
Chapter 5 (Lineage and Insights) and Chapter 6 (Governance Workflows)
Chapter 6 (Governance Workflows) and Chapter 7 (Purview in Practice)
questions.explain: The three-step shape is: find it (Chapters 1-2, foundations and the Data Map), trust it (Chapters 3-4, classification and the catalog), govern it (Chapters 5-6, lineage and workflows), with Chapter 7 applying all three to one case study.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement among Lesson 35's five best-practice habits.
options: Scope first — start with collections and data products matching real organizational boundaries, not the entire estate at once
Scan before you classify, since a classification can't flag anything in a table that's never been scanned
Define before you build — write a glossary term before a dashboard gets built on top of it
The same person should both author and publish a policy, to move faster
A perfectly governed catalog that nobody actually searches has already solved the governance problem
questions.explain: Scope first, scan before you classify, and define before you build are three of the five genuine habits from Lesson 35. The lesson explicitly recommends splitting policy authoring from publishing, not combining them, as a checks-and-balances pattern. And it explicitly states a perfectly governed catalog nobody searches 'hasn't solved anything' — adoption is the point, not a side effect.
